Ces Ukraniens que l’on oublie : journal: The Ukrainians We Forget: A Roma Logbook
La guerre sévit, mais elle n’est pas véc: The war rages on, but not everyone experiences it the same way. How is it affecting the country’s most vulnerable population: the Roma?
Depuis le 24 février 2022, les cachettes: Since February 24, 2022, hiding in underground shelters has become part of daily life for many Ukrainians. The war rages on, but not everyone experiences it the same way. How is it affecting the country’s most vulnerable population: the Roma? The Ukrainians we forget tell us their stories. It is Friday. It is midnight in Ukraine.
‍<strong>Jour 2</strong> de la guerre. J: ‍Day 2 of the war. Julian Kondur has left his home in Kyiv to hide in a small village not far from the city, where the bombings are less frequent, but still happening. He takes a few minutes to speak with us; he wants the world to know what is going on there. “I can talk to you, but if something happens, I’ll have to drop the phone and go back to my hiding place,” he says right away. “Today, the reality for the Roma is no different from that of Ukrainians,” says the coordinator of the Ukrainian Roma organization Chirikli. “We all want to stay with our families and defend our homes.”
Samedi après-midi, <strong>jour 3.</stro: Saturday afternoon, day 3. Sasha (not his real name) has had a long night. A few days before the invasion of Ukraine, he was in England, visiting his sister. Instead of returning home, the journalist took refuge in Slovakia at his mother-in-law’s. On Friday evening, his wife and daughter joined him from Ukraine, under the sound of bombs. They managed to cross the Slovak border. Sasha insists that Ukraine’s Roma are helping the Ukrainian resistance and that this help is visible across the country. He sends us photos of Ukrainian Roma soldiers. Despite the racism and discrimination the community faces, Sasha hopes the war will stir a sense of patriotism and unity throughout the country. He is not afraid that the community will be doubly victimized by the war, as it was during the war in Kosovo, where it was persecuted by both sides. “The Roma are soldiers too, we belong here in Ukraine, we don’t want to go to another country, we want to stay in Ukraine, where we were raised and where we have raised our children.”
<sup>Nataliia Tomenko n’a plus la notion: Nataliia Tomenko has lost track of time. It is hard for her to tell us what day of the week it is. She only knows it is the fourth day of the war. Nataliia and her family are in central Ukraine. She says that she and her loved ones are relatively safe. But she spends her nights in a cellar, woken by the sound of the alert sirens announcing bombs. Her distress is obvious. “Yesterday, I couldn’t explain to my year-and-a-half-old niece why we had to quickly barricade ourselves in this cold, dark cellar and sit there for hours because the alarm that signals the bombs had started to sound. I tried to turn it into a game of hide-and-seek, but she could feel the fear, a fear I can also see in the eyes of every member of my family,” she says to the camera, her eyes filled with tears. To be able to sleep, the young woman takes sleeping pills. “I’ve started to appreciate simple words like hello and good night. That special feeling when you go to bed and wish for a calm, quiet night, and you hope to wake up alive and be able to say hello to your family in the morning. I hope we will be able to survive,” she says. In the streets, Roma and non-Roma Ukrainians are defending their country together against the Russian forces. Nataliia Tomenko calls for unity: “The Roma are Ukrainians too. People must stay united now, because this is the time to help one another. In the streets, Roma and non-Roma Ukrainians are fighting side by side for their country.” But despite the patriotism and bravery of this visible minority, it still faces discrimination. Nataliia describes how classmates told her 12-year-old sister, “Shut up, you Gypsy*,” as she was sharing her fears in an online discussion group set up by her school to support students during the war. “Even in these moments, Roma children are exposed to hatred. I answered the kids by telling them: ‘Now is the time to unite, we must stay together,’” she says. “We are afraid, for every member of my family, for every person in Ukraine, for every member of the Roma community – everyone, help us!” implores the artist and researcher, her voice choked with emotion.
<strong>La situation des Roms en Ukraine: The situation of the Roma in Ukraine
Il y aurait de 250 000 à 400 000 Roms uk: There are an estimated 250,000 to 400,000 Roma living in Ukraine. Nearly <l1>40,000 of them have no identity papers</l1>. Many live in isolated Roma neighbourhoods, in extreme poverty. They are the most vulnerable minority in Ukraine, where a long history of anti-Roma violence persists. Even today, anti-Roma racism is widespread and accepted by the Ukrainian population and politicians.
Depuis quelques années, une vague de pog: In recent years, a wave of pogroms has swept over the community. Roma have been driven from their homes and killed in front of local police officers who, at times, take part in these crimes. Last fall, nearly 50 members of the far right targeted the community during a demonstration in the city of Irpin. Neo-Nazis from the group C14 chanted hateful slogans, calling for violence against the city’s Roma. The group also painted hateful messages on the fence of a Roma family’s home.
<l1>En 2018 à Lviv, les paramilitaires d: <l1>In 2018 in Lviv, C14 paramilitaries attacked </l1>Roma women and young children with cayenne pepper in a camp after burning down their homes. A 24-year-old man, David Pap, died, and several people were seriously injured. <l2>No one has yet been convicted for this attack.</l2> In 2017, a community leader was shot dead by members of far-right groups in Kharkiv. To this day, no one has been charged for the murder. According to a Human Rights Watch report, official investigations rarely produce results.
Selon <l1>un rapport de 2019 de Minority: According to <l1>a 2019 Minority Rights Group report</l1> on the situation of the Roma in Ukraine, local and national Ukrainian authorities consider their marginalization in the country a secondary problem, compared with the security and governance issues Ukraine faces amid Russian aggression, economic hardship and radical reforms. Several Roma organizations in Ukraine work to raise awareness among their governments and institutions. But since the invasion, they fear that their suffering will be exploited by Russian forces, who officially aim to “denazify Ukraine.”
Avec le racisme anti-rom qui est fort ré: With anti-Roma racism so widespread in Europe, Roma organizations fear that the minority will not receive the same help as other Ukrainian citizens. Natalia Tomenko says she fears that antiziganism in Ukraine will worsen with the war. “As we know, in many countries, when wars begin, Roma communities are among the most vulnerable and can be attacked and targeted from several sides. I’m very afraid for the members of our community,” says the activist.
<strong>‍</strong>Les témoignages commen: ‍Testimonies are starting to come in. Ukrainian Roma are facing discrimination at borders in Eastern Europe. In some cases, they are denied basic services, say the Roma activists we speak with who are on the ground in Europe. In Chisinau, Moldova, I reach Nicolae Radita. At the city’s request, he guides refugees arriving from Ukraine and provides them with assistance. “At first, people didn’t pay attention to differences in social class and economic differences. But now that the number of refugees is growing, spaces are becoming scarcer. So the Moldovan state has started to be more selective,” says the Roma lawyer, who works at the Council of Europe on projects related to hate crimes.
À MoldExpo, un centre d’exposition trans: At MoldExpo, an exhibition centre converted into a reception centre for refugees, goods such as food, clothing, diapers and donations are sorted. “Sometimes there are cases of mistreatment. Some people say openly: ‘Gypsies*, shut up!’” According to Radita, many Roma are afraid to ask for help. “Roma, who are refugees too, went to ask for food and diapers for their children. But the staff started to refuse; they only refused help to the Roma,” Radita tells us, adding that he raised the issue with local officials. They told him that Roma had to provide proof of refugee status to obtain goods. But according to the lawyer, only the Roma are asked for this proof. He believes that the Moldovan authorities are using arbitrary methods to make it much harder to support Roma refugees from Ukraine. He cites the example of Roma from Moldova who have lived in Ukraine for several years and still have not obtained Ukrainian citizenship.
En arrivant à Chisinau, fuyant la guerre: On arriving in Chisinau, fleeing the war, some find themselves facing people who refuse to take care of them on the pretext that help is reserved for Ukrainian citizens. “It’s against the law, the Moldovan state has said that anyone arriving from Ukraine has the right to be taken care of,” says the lawyer. According to <l1>a report by the European Roma Rights Centre</l1>, Ukrainian Roma refugees are being segregated in shelters in Moldova. Those without identity papers are often stuck in these centres, unable to join family or friends in other countries or to return to Ukraine. Faced with this situation, many people try to leave the refugee centres, thinking they will find better conditions elsewhere. But they run up against the racism of the local population.
Nicolae Radita nous raconte le périple d: Nicolae Radita tells us about the ordeal of a group of Roma refugees in Chisinau. “They saw that the authorities were starting to prioritize certain people and that conditions weren’t very good. So they began looking for shelter themselves. I told them about offers circulating among the public. They called the people who were offering shelter. On the phone, they were told there was room,” he says. The experience on site was quite different. “When the shelter owners saw that the group was made up of Roma, they told them there was no more room.” The scenario repeated itself elsewhere. After several attempts, a student residence agreed to take in the group. Another incident happened on the day of our call. “Today, the members of one family came. They had been offered shelter over the phone. But when the owner saw them, he said: ‘I don’t want Roma, Roma are bad, they don’t know how to organize themselves, I don’t want to host them here.’” Black, Indian, Arab and Asian international students have faced similar exclusion since the start of the war, as several media outlets and students on social media have reported.
En Moldavie, Nicolae Radita pense que le: In Moldova, Nicolae Radita believes the treatment reserved for the Roma is different. “I wouldn’t say international students are treated better, it’s different; people understand that they’ll only stay a few days. With the Roma, there’s a fear that they’ll stay.” Pointing to centuries of normalized anti-Roma racism in Eastern Europe, Radita explains that while many civil society activists think Roma refugees should speak out about these situations on social media, the most vulnerable simply have no such intention. “They’re not asking for justice; for them, it’s not so much a matter of principle, it’s a need.” After nightfall, we talk with Gregori Rota, who left Odessa, Ukraine, on February 25 with 27 members of his family. He feels that he was treated differently on arriving in Chisinau. “People avoid us, they don’t come near us,” he says. His family therefore looked for shelter in private accommodations. Gregori describes how they were refused places. After three tries, he managed to find shelter with Moldovan Roma families. His family had to split up to find refuge in four different houses.
Certains de ses amis roms sont restés au: Some of his Roma friends stayed at the MoldExpo centre. Gregori is trying to help them. “They called us to say they weren’t being given anything to eat. I went there with my wife, but the people who work there wouldn’t let us bring them food. They also wouldn’t let the families go out to get the food we wanted to give them. They said they were going to call the police,” says the refugee.
Le chauffeur Jaroslav Miko discute avec: Driver Jaroslav Miko talks with the families he is transporting on his bus. Photo: Petr Salaba
<strong>‍</strong>À Prague, Jaroslav Mik: ‍In Prague, Jaroslav Miko, who is half Czech, half Roma, is a bus driver. He volunteers for the organization Češi pomáhají (Czech aid) and goes to pick up Ukrainian refugees in Slovakia. On his first visit to the Slovak-Ukrainian border, he notices that the buses are only taking white Ukrainians. Jaroslav decides to make round trips to transport those who are being left behind, like the Roma. “Yesterday, I saw a group of Roma who had no transportation. There were pregnant women and people with disabilities among them. The drivers said their buses were too new and clean, that the Roma were dirty, that they didn’t deserve to sit in them. They said they were afraid they would destroy their bus,” he says.
Pour contrer les conséquences de cette d: To counter the consequences of this discrimination, the driver shuttles between the Czech Republic and Slovakia every day. With the Czech organization he volunteers for, he managed to secure the support of the Czech government to help Roma refugees. Recently, he transported a group of 150 Roma women and children who had been looking for a driver for three days – no one wanted to take them. So far, he has helped a little over 500 Ukrainian Roma refugees leave Slovakia for the Czech Republic. Behind his steering wheel, he observes the differences. According to him, white Ukrainians are taken to various shelters in Slovakia, while the Roma end up in tents at the Humenné refugee camp. Others also describe this situation.
En Slovaquie, le colonel Mariàn Pouchan: In Slovakia, Colonel Mariàn Pouchan <l1>lashed out at Roma families </l1>saying they were taking advantage of the humanitarian aid offered by the country and should not have the right to cross the border. Peter Bucka, a social worker of Roma origin who lives in Prague, laments that refugees from the community can only count on other Roma in Europe to support them. “Roma in the Czech Republic and Slovakia have organized to help our community. It’s as if Eastern European countries don’t want any more Roma from elsewhere. There are already Roma from Slovakia living there, and they don’t want any more.” He says the situation is worse in Poland, where there are fewer Roma organizations that can mobilize to help the community. At the time of our call, transport is suspended for a 24-hour period. Jaroslav Miko wants to continue his work helping Roma refugees from Ukraine. His commitment does not stop there; he also wants to approach the Minister of the Interior and the shelter directors to make sure that the Roma do not end up on the street and are taken care of by the Czech state. “I feel accountable to people. It’s not possible, in the 21st century, for families to be stranded on the street. It’s indecent, especially for the children. In a way, it’s a failure of the state,” he says.
Une femme rom montre sur son téléphone,: A Roma woman shows on her phone a photo of her brother, who joined the Ukrainian forces. Photo: Petr Salaba
<strong>‍</strong>Sasha nous donne des n: ‍Sasha gives us an update. “Please call me,” he writes. He is afraid to put his name on reports. A week has passed since our first interview. The journalist is still in Slovakia with his family. He is in touch with several Ukrainian Roma in Eastern Europe and shares his observations with us. “Now everything has changed, there is a lot, a lot of discrimination against the Roma everywhere,” he tells us right away by video call. “On trains in Ukraine, Roma, even when they show their passport, are told: ‘Get lost, get lost, go to the Gypsies*, they’ll help you,’” he says as an example. He adds that some Roma women are returning to Ukraine with their children, despite the war. “They prefer to live in fear alongside their husbands rather than in segregation and insecurity,” the journalist explains.
En Ukraine, la guerre n’atténue pas les: In Ukraine, the war is not easing racial discrimination. Sasha tells us the story of his sister, who also decided to go back to Ukraine while she was at the border. “There was a young Roma boy who asked for water, and a soldier told him: ‘Open your mouth, and I’ll piss in it,’” Sasha says hesitantly. When she reached the Ukrainian border, Sasha’s sister noticed that many Roma were lining up to go to Slovakia. But Ukrainian border guards were making them wait. They would be the last to cross. Sasha’s mother called him from Ukraine. She was in shock. “It’s really everywhere, even in essential services, in solidarity: the priority is white Ukrainians. If you have dark skin, it’s a disaster,” he says, as is often the case for the Roma community in Eastern Europe. In Uzhhorod, in western Ukraine, the bombings are less frequent. Many Roma and non-Roma Ukrainians from Kharkiv and other regions more heavily attacked by the Russians are moving there. The Roma minority does not get the same welcome. “Residents tell Roma refugees: ‘Leave, go to the Gypsies*, they’ll help you,’” Sasha explains.
Dans le quartier de Telmana, où on trouv: In the Telmana neighbourhood, where there is a Roma population, there were already tensions between Ukrainians and Roma before the war. But since the start of the conflict, they have worsened. On February 26, Roma residents were attacked, and five people were shot. Two of them are in intensive care, another is in a coma. Since the incident, local police have been patrolling the neighbourhood. We return to the conversation we had a few days earlier, when we were talking about Roma soldiers. Sasha had said he wasn’t afraid that Ukraine’s Roma community would suffer the same fate as the Roma in Kosovo during the war. He has changed his mind. “Everything has changed; we’re really afraid of what will happen. Many Roma are staying to protect Ukraine, but it’s hard, when you’re staying to protect your country, to feel this racism.” For Sasha and so many others, the war has no colour, but the obstacles are different for the most vulnerable. “This war is a war between Ukraine and Russia. It’s not like the Second World War, when it was a racial war against Jews and Roma. But now, people are starting to be treated differently depending on their skin colour, their ethnicity.”
Que fait alors la communauté devant cett: What is the community doing in the face of this injustice? “Nothing, we’re starting to help one another, we don’t feel protected,” replies the journalist, a week after the Russian invasion. Sasha leaves us with a message for those who are suffering from this war and those who are taking them in: “Be careful, aven manusha, be human, even in difference.”
Lors de la <l1>rencontre d’urgence du Co: At the <l1>emergency meeting of the United Nations Human Rights Council</l1> on March 4, Julian Kondur issued a call for solidarity and action in an <l2>open letter</l2> signed by more than 400 Romani and non-Romani organizations and individuals. The collective expressed its concerns about the war in Ukraine and decided to mobilize so that no one is left behind. “From the Second World War to the Balkan wars of the late 1990s, history has shown us that in times of war or conflict, the fate of the Romani community and other minorities is continually ignored,” the letter reads. Here are the collective’s demands:
On demande aux autorités et aux interven: Authorities and humanitarian workers are asked to ensure that Roma, minorities and marginalized people, including those without identity documents, have equal access to protection and safety when they seek refuge.
On demande aux gouvernements, dirigeants: Governments, world leaders, and international, regional and European institutions and organizations are asked to examine the human rights violations and violence suffered by Roma and other vulnerable communities, and to investigate allegations of discrimination against them by Ukrainian and/or European authorities when they seek protection and asylum at the borders.
On demande aux médias de ne pas exploite: The media are asked not to exploit the war against Ukraine to promote inflammatory and racist depictions of marginalized groups, which would further stigmatize them and increase the risk of violence against them.
On demande aux instances des Nations uni: United Nations bodies are asked to establish a commission of inquiry capable of monitoring the human rights violations and violence suffered by Roma and other minorities, who have often been doubly victimized by the war.
<strong><em>*Tzigane, gitan : </em></str: *Tzigane, gitan: In Eastern Europe, the word “tzigane” (Gypsy) has a pejorative connotation. It is a racial slur. The word was used during the enslavement of the Roma. It comes from the Greek word athinganos, meaning “untouchable” or “impure.” Calling a Romani person a Gypsy in a European context, especially in the east, is condescending. The term “gitan” is also considered a racial slur. The correct term to use for this people is “Rom.”
